misconceptions.statement: Rusting is just dirt or a stain settling on the iron surface.
misconceptions.why: Rust looks like a brown deposit, so it seems like something that sticks on from outside.
misconceptions.fix: Rust is a new substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water; it is a chemical change.

probe.question: Rust on a nail is just dirt that settled on it. True or false?
probe.wrong_answer: True, wiping it off leaves the same iron as before.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you see on the surface is just added matter

misconceptions.statement: Rusting is a physical change because iron stays the same metal.
misconceptions.why: Students see the object remain, only changed in colour, and equate colour change with physical change.
misconceptions.fix: Rusting is a chemical change because a new substance, iron oxide, forms and cannot be turned back into iron easily.

probe.question: Is rusting a physical or a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Physical, because the iron is still there.

misconceptions.root_belief: if the object looks similar, nothing really changed
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas about chemical change and conservation of substance

misconceptions.statement: All metals rust when left in damp air.
misconceptions.why: The word rusting is used loosely for any metal getting spoilt.
misconceptions.fix: Rusting is specific to iron and its alloys like steel; other metals corrode in different ways, such as silver tarnishing or copper turning green.

probe.question: Does a copper vessel left in damp air rust?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all metals rust in damp air.

misconceptions.root_belief: what happens to one example happens to all

misconceptions.statement: Rust and corrosion mean exactly the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Everyday language uses both words interchangeably.
misconceptions.fix: Corrosion is the general slow eating away of metals; rusting is the particular corrosion of iron.

probe.question: Silver turns black in air. Is this rusting?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is rusting since the metal is corroding.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Iron rusts with only water; air is not needed.
misconceptions.why: Students notice rust where water is visible and forget that air supplies oxygen.
misconceptions.fix: Iron needs both oxygen from air and water; without either it does not rust.

probe.question: A nail is placed in boiled water under an oil layer. Will it rust?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is in water.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' single-factor explanations of rusting

misconceptions.statement: Air has no role since gases cannot affect a solid metal.
misconceptions.why: Gases are invisible and seem too light to matter.
misconceptions.fix: Oxygen in air is a reactant, and it combines with iron to form rust.

probe.question: Does a nail in dry air with a drying agent rust?
probe.wrong_answer: No role for air, so any rusting must come from the nail itself.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas of gases as having no mass or role

misconceptions.statement: A nail in a sealed tube with plain tap water won't rust because there is no fresh air.
misconceptions.why: Students think air must keep flowing in, ignoring dissolved air in water.
misconceptions.fix: Ordinary water has dissolved oxygen and the tube has air above it, so the nail rusts; only boiled water with oil lacks oxygen.

probe.question: A nail sits in unboiled water in a closed tube. Rust?
probe.wrong_answer: No, no fresh air gets in.

misconceptions.root_belief: only visible flowing supply counts

misconceptions.statement: Calcium chloride in the tube gives the nail the water it needs.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse a drying agent with a wetting agent because it is a salt.
misconceptions.fix: Calcium chloride absorbs moisture and keeps the air dry, so the nail does not rust.

probe.question: A nail is in dry air with calcium chloride. Does it rust?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the salt helps rusting.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Rust is pure iron that has turned brown.
misconceptions.why: Colour change is read as the same substance in a different shade.
misconceptions.fix: Rust is hydrated iron oxide, a compound of iron, oxygen and water.

probe.question: What is rust made of?
probe.wrong_answer: Iron only, just brown.

misconceptions.root_belief: changed appearance means same substance
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students treating reaction products as the original substance

misconceptions.statement: Rust is made of water only, since water causes it.
misconceptions.why: Students link the cause with the product directly.
misconceptions.fix: Rust is a compound of iron with oxygen and water; iron is part of it.

probe.question: Which element forms the main part of rust?
probe.wrong_answer: Water.

misconceptions.root_belief: the cause is the same as the product

misconceptions.statement: A layer of rust protects the iron under it from further rusting.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise from aluminium oxide or from paint-like coating ideas.
misconceptions.fix: Rust is flaky and porous, so it falls off or lets air and water through, and rusting continues deeper.

probe.question: Will a thick layer of rust stop the iron beneath from rusting?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it covers the iron like a coat.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Rusting makes an iron object heavier in size but never weakens it.
misconceptions.why: Students see more brown material and think matter is added, not iron lost.
misconceptions.fix: Rusting eats away the iron, making objects weak and brittle, even though rust is bulky.

probe.question: A rusted bridge beam looks thicker. Is it stronger?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more material means stronger.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Rust can be turned back into iron by just rubbing or washing it off.
misconceptions.why: Students think rust is only on the surface and the iron below is untouched.
misconceptions.fix: Rubbing removes rust but the iron lost is gone; rust is a different compound and cannot be washed back into iron.

probe.question: If you scrub off rust, is the nail as good as before?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the nail is the same as new.

misconceptions.root_belief: changes only affect the surface

misconceptions.statement: Salt water makes iron rust only because it has more water.
misconceptions.why: Students think the effect comes from quantity of water, not the dissolved salt.
misconceptions.fix: Dissolved salts make water conduct better and speed the chemical reaction, so rusting is faster in salt water.

probe.question: Why do ships rust faster in sea water than in a river?
probe.wrong_answer: Sea has more water.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Salt itself is a rust, so salt water turns iron into rust directly.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up speeding up a change with doing the change.
misconceptions.fix: Salt is not needed for rusting; it only makes rusting faster because iron still needs oxygen and water.

probe.question: Will iron rust in dry salt with no water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, salt alone rusts iron.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Salt is used up when it makes iron rust faster.
misconceptions.why: Students expect any helper in a change to get consumed like a reactant.
misconceptions.fix: Salt only speeds up rusting and is not part of rust, so it is not used up.

probe.question: Does the salt in sea water get used up while making iron rust?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it becomes part of the rust.

misconceptions.root_belief: anything involved in a change is used up

misconceptions.statement: Paint stops rusting because it makes the iron stronger.
misconceptions.why: Painting feels like strengthening or hardening the surface.
misconceptions.fix: Paint is a barrier that keeps air and moisture away from iron; if it peels, iron rusts.

probe.question: Why does painting a gate prevent rusting?
probe.wrong_answer: It makes the iron stronger.

misconceptions.root_belief: a coating changes the thing itself

misconceptions.statement: A scratched painted iron object stays fully protected.
misconceptions.why: Students think the surrounding paint still protects the exposed patch.
misconceptions.fix: A scratch exposes iron to air and moisture, so rust begins there and can spread under the paint.

probe.question: A painted grill has a deep scratch. Will it stay rust free?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the paint still protects it.

misconceptions.root_belief: the whole acts the same even if part fails

misconceptions.statement: Galvanised iron does not rust because zinc does not react with anything.
misconceptions.why: Students assume protective coating metals are inert.
misconceptions.fix: Zinc is more reactive than iron and reacts first, protecting the iron beneath it.

probe.question: Why does zinc coating protect iron?
probe.wrong_answer: Zinc is unreactive.

misconceptions.root_belief: protecting means being unreactive
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas of sacrificial protection and reactivity

misconceptions.statement: If the zinc layer gets scratched, the exposed iron will rust like unprotected iron.
misconceptions.why: Students treat zinc as only a paint-like barrier.
misconceptions.fix: Zinc is more reactive, so it keeps protecting exposed iron nearby even when scratched.

probe.question: A galvanised pipe is scratched. Will the bare iron rust fast?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, as with painted iron.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Stainless steel is pure iron that has been polished or painted.
misconceptions.why: The shiny surface suggests a surface treatment of iron.
misconceptions.fix: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with carbon, chromium and nickel, so the whole metal resists rusting.

probe.question: What is stainless steel made of?
probe.wrong_answer: Iron with a coat of polish.

misconceptions.root_belief: properties come from surface not composition

misconceptions.statement: Silver turns black because it rusts.
misconceptions.why: Rusting is the only metal spoiling word students know.
misconceptions.fix: Silver tarnishes by reacting with sulphur compounds in air to form black silver sulphide.

probe.question: What makes silver jewellery turn black?
probe.wrong_answer: It rusts in air and water.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' use of rusting for all metal corrosion

misconceptions.statement: The green coating on copper is copper rust, made like iron rust from oxygen and water.
misconceptions.why: Students extend the iron rusting pattern to copper.
misconceptions.fix: The green coating is basic copper carbonate formed with oxygen, carbon dioxide and moisture of air.

probe.question: What gases of air are needed for green coating on copper?
probe.wrong_answer: Only oxygen and water.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Aluminium does not corrode at all, so it never reacts with air.
misconceptions.why: Aluminium objects stay shiny for years.
misconceptions.fix: Aluminium reacts quickly with air to form a thin oxide layer that protects the metal below.

probe.question: Does aluminium react with oxygen of air?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it never reacts.

misconceptions.root_belief: no visible change means no reaction
